records.source: וַיַּ֗עַל נָחָשׁ֙ הָֽעַמּוֹנִ֔י וַיִּ֖חַן עַל־יָבֵ֣שׁ גִּלְעָ֑ד וַיֹּ֨אמְר֜וּ כָּל־אַנְשֵׁ֤י יָבֵישׁ֙ אֶל־נָחָ֔שׁ כְּרָת־לָ֥נוּ בְרִ֖ית וְנַעַבְדֶֽךָּ׃
records.gloss: And went up Nahash the Ammonite and encamped against Jabesh-gilead; and said all [the] men of Jabesh to Nahash, Make for us a covenant, and we will serve you.
pieces: Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh told Nahash, "If you make a treaty with us, we will be subject to you."

L.1: And Nahash the Ammonite went up and encamped against Jabesh-gilead. And all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you."

R.1: Nahash, the king of the Ammonites, marched against the town of Jabesh-gilead and surrounded it. All the men of Jabesh said to him, "Make a peace agreement with us, and we will be your subjects."

decisions.choice: the chapter begins with Nahash's attack, with no account of what came before it
alternatives: a longer introduction telling of Nahash's earlier attacks on Gad and Reuben
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text, which this translation follows, moves straight from 10:27 to the siege. One Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel (known as 4QSam-a) has a longer passage at this point: Nahash had been oppressing the tribes of Gad and Reuben east of the Jordan, gouging out every man's right eye, and some seven thousand men had escaped from him into Jabesh-gilead. The old Greek translation also reads "about a month later" where the Hebrew of 10:27 ends "but he kept silent". The longer passage may be original and lost from the Hebrew by a copying slip, or it may be an early expansion. Reviewers should check the wording against the scroll's published text.

decisions.choice: Nahash the Ammonite: the king of Ammon, the people living east of the Jordan around Rabbah
decisions.reason: Samuel later calls him "Nahash king of the Ammonites" (12:12), and his son Hanun followed him on the throne (2 Samuel 10:1-2). Ammon had long claimed the land of Gilead east of the Jordan (Judges 11:4-33), where Jabesh lay.

decisions.choice: Jabesh-gilead: the town in Gilead whose people had been bound to Benjamin since Judges 21
decisions.reason: After Israel's war with Benjamin, four hundred young women of Jabesh-gilead became wives for the surviving men of Benjamin (Judges 21:8-14). That tie helps explain why the messengers go to Gibeah, Saul's town in Benjamin (verse 4), and why the people of Jabesh later risk their lives to bury Saul (31:11-13).

decisions.choice: make a covenant with us, and we will serve you: accept us as subjects on terms
decisions.reason: The town offers to surrender and become subject to Nahash, paying tribute, in return for a treaty that would spare their lives. A covenant between a strong king and a weak people set out the duties of each side.

decisions.choice: covenant (Literal); treaty (Balanced); peace agreement (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word is the usual one for covenant. Here it is an agreement between a conquering king and a town, so Balanced says "treaty" and Readable "peace agreement". "We will serve you" is put as becoming his subjects at both levels, and Balanced turns the offer into an "if" clause, which is how the two halves relate.

decisions.choice: the king of the Ammonites
decisions.reason: Readable supplies Nahash's title from 12:12 so the reader knows who he is.

records.heading: Nahash threatens Jabesh-gilead

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֗ם נָחָשׁ֙ הָעַמּוֹנִ֔י בְּזֹאת֙ אֶכְרֹ֣ת לָכֶ֔ם בִּנְק֥וֹר לָכֶ֖ם כָּל־עֵ֣ין יָמִ֑ין וְשַׂמְתִּ֥יהָ חֶרְפָּ֖ה עַל־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And said to them Nahash the Ammonite, On this I will make [it] with you, by gouging out for you every right eye, and I will make it a reproach on all Israel.
pieces: But Nahash the Ammonite answered them, "I will make a treaty with you, but only on this condition: I will gouge out the right eye of every one of you. In this way I will bring disgrace on all Israel."

L.2: And Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this [condition] I will make [a covenant] with you: by gouging out every right eye of yours; and I will make it a disgrace on all Israel."

R.2: Nahash answered, "I will make an agreement with you only if I can put out the right eye of each of you. That will bring shame on all of Israel."

decisions.choice: on this I will make [a covenant]: these are my terms
decisions.reason: Nahash repeats the verb "make" from verse 1 without its object; "covenant" is understood. "On this" points ahead to the condition he names.

decisions.choice: gouging out every right eye: a mutilation meant to humiliate a conquered people
decisions.reason: Blinding or maiming captives was a known way of shaming and disabling them (Judges 1:6-7; 16:21). Losing the right eye would also leave a man less able to fight, since a soldier holding a shield on his left side looks past it with his right eye. Nahash says his main purpose plainly: to disgrace all Israel.

decisions.choice: reproach: public shame and scorn
decisions.reason: The word names the disgrace a people bears when others mock its defeat. The mutilated men of Jabesh would be a living sign of Israel's weakness.

decisions.choice: on one condition
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the condition explicit, which the Literal level marks with brackets.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ אֵלָ֜יו זִקְנֵ֣י יָבֵ֗ישׁ הֶ֤רֶף לָ֨נוּ֙ שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֔ים וְנִשְׁלְחָה֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל גְּב֣וּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְאִם־אֵ֥ין מוֹשִׁ֛יעַ אֹתָ֖נוּ וְיָצָ֥אנוּ אֵלֶֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: And said to him [the] elders of Jabesh, Let alone us seven days, and we will send messengers into all [the] territory of Israel, and if there is no one saving us, then we will come out to you.
pieces: The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days, so that we can send messengers throughout the territory of Israel. Then, if no one comes to rescue us, we will come out and surrender to you."

L.3: And the elders of Jabesh said to him, "Leave us alone seven days, so that we may send messengers into all the territory of Israel; and if there is no one to save us, we will come out to you."

R.3: The leaders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days to send messengers all over Israel. If no one comes to save us, we will come out and give ourselves up to you."

decisions.choice: leave us alone: hold off from us
decisions.reason: The verb means to let go or let drop. The elders ask Nahash to hold back his attack for seven days. That he agrees shows how sure he is that no one will come.

decisions.choice: one who saves: a rescuer like the judges
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for the deliverers Yahweh raised up in Judges, such as Othniel and Ehud (Judges 3:9, 15). The question of the chapter is who will play that part now that Israel has a king.

decisions.choice: come out to you: surrender
decisions.reason: To come out of a besieged city to the enemy is to give oneself up (2 Kings 18:31; 24:12). The same words return with a double meaning in verse 10.

decisions.choice: leaders
decisions.reason: Readable says "leaders" for the elders, the senior men who spoke for the town.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֤אוּ הַמַּלְאָכִים֙ גִּבְעַ֣ת שָׁא֔וּל וַיְדַבְּר֥וּ הַדְּבָרִ֖ים בְּאָזְנֵ֣י הָעָ֑ם וַיִּשְׂא֧וּ כָל־הָעָ֛ם אֶת־קוֹלָ֖ם וַיִּבְכּֽוּ׃
records.gloss: And came the messengers [to] Gibeah of Saul, and spoke the words in [the] ears of the people, and lifted up all the people their voice and wept.
pieces: When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and told the people what had happened, all the people wept aloud.

L.4: And the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and spoke the words in the ears of the people, and all the people lifted up their voice and wept.

R.4: The messengers came to Gibeah, the town where Saul lived, and told the people there what was happening. Everyone began to cry loudly.

decisions.choice: Gibeah of Saul: Saul's home town in Benjamin
decisions.reason: Saul had gone home to Gibeah after he was chosen king (10:26). The town was a few miles north of Jerusalem. The messengers may have gone first to Benjamin because of the old bond between Jabesh and that tribe (see verse 1).

decisions.choice: spoke in the ears of the people ... lifted up their voice and wept: told them publicly ... wept aloud
decisions.reason: "In the ears of" means in the hearing of. "Lifted up their voice and wept" describes loud mourning, as when Israel wept at Bochim (Judges 2:4). The people weep but do nothing: no one yet acts to save Jabesh.

decisions.choice: the town where Saul lived
decisions.reason: Readable explains "Gibeah of Saul" so the reader sees why the place is named after him.

records.source: וְהִנֵּ֣ה שָׁא֗וּל בָּ֣א אַחֲרֵ֤י הַבָּקָר֙ מִן־הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל מַה־לָּעָ֖ם כִּ֣י יִבְכּ֑וּ וַיְסַ֨פְּרוּ־ל֔וֹ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֖י אַנְשֵׁ֥י יָבֵֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And look, Saul [was] coming after the cattle from the field, and said Saul, What [is] to the people that they weep? And they told him [the] words of [the] men of Jabesh.
pieces: Just then Saul was coming in from the field behind his oxen. He asked, "What is wrong with the people? Why are they weeping?" They told him what the men of Jabesh had said.

L.5: And look, Saul was coming behind the cattle from the field. And Saul said, "What is [wrong] with the people that they are weeping?" And they told him the words of the men of Jabesh.

R.5: Just then Saul was coming in from the field, walking behind his oxen. "Why is everyone crying?" he asked. So they told him the message from the men of Jabesh.

decisions.choice: look: the narrator turns attention to Saul arriving at that moment
decisions.reason: The word points to something seen as it happens. Saul walks onto the scene just as the town is weeping.

decisions.choice: Saul was coming behind the cattle: he was still working his family's land
decisions.reason: Though Samuel had anointed him and the people had acclaimed him king (10:1, 24), Saul had no court yet and was back at work as a farmer. The oxen he is driving become the means of his call to Israel in verse 7.

decisions.choice: cattle: here plowing oxen
decisions.reason: The word is a general one for cattle. Verse 7 speaks of a "yoke" of them, so these are draft oxen used for plowing.

decisions.choice: oxen
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "oxen" because the animals are a plowing team (verse 7); Literal keeps the general word "cattle".

records.source: וַתִּצְלַ֤ח רֽוּחַ־אֱלֹהִים֙ עַל־שָׁא֔וּל כְּשָׁמְע֖וֹ אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּ֥חַר אַפּ֖וֹ מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And rushed [the] Spirit of God on Saul when he heard these words, and burned his anger greatly.
pieces: When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God rushed on him, and he became very angry.

L.6: And the Spirit of God rushed on Saul when he heard these words, and his anger burned greatly.

R.6: When Saul heard this, the Spirit of God rushed on him, and he became furious.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of God rushed on Saul: came on him suddenly and with power
decisions.reason: The same verb is used when the Spirit came on Saul among the prophets (10:6, 10) and on Samson before his great acts (Judges 14:6, 19; 15:14). As with the judges, God's Spirit equips Saul to lead Israel in rescue.

decisions.choice: his anger burned greatly: he became very angry
decisions.reason: "His anger burned" is the usual Hebrew way of saying someone became angry. Here it is anger roused by the Spirit against the cruelty and insult of Nahash.

records.source: וַיִּקַּח֩ צֶ֨מֶד בָּקָ֜ר וַֽיְנַתְּחֵ֗הוּ וַיְשַׁלַּ֞ח בְּכָל־גְּב֣וּל יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ בְּיַ֣ד הַמַּלְאָכִ֣ים׀לֵאמֹר֒ אֲשֶׁר֩ אֵינֶ֨נּוּ יֹצֵ֜א אַחֲרֵ֤י שָׁאוּל֙ וְאַחַ֣ר שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל כֹּ֥ה יֵעָשֶׂ֖ה לִבְקָר֑וֹ וַיִּפֹּ֤ל פַּֽחַד־יְהוָה֙ עַל־הָעָ֔ם וַיֵּצְא֖וּ כְּאִ֥ישׁ אֶחָֽד׃
records.gloss: And he took a yoke of cattle and cut it in pieces and sent [them] in all [the] territory of Israel by [the] hand of the messengers, saying, Whoever is not coming out after Saul and after Samuel, thus it will be done to his cattle. And fell [the] dread of Yahweh on the people, and they came out as one man.
pieces: He took a yoke of oxen and cut them up, and he sent the pieces by the messengers through all the territory of Israel with this message: "Anyone who does not come out behind Saul and Samuel will have the same done to his oxen." Then the dread of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} fell on the people, and they came out as one man.

L.7: And he took a yoke of cattle and cut them in pieces and sent [them] through all the territory of Israel by the hand of the messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and after Samuel, so will it be done to his cattle." And the dread of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} fell on the people, and they came out as one man.

R.7: Saul took two of his oxen and cut them into pieces. He gave the pieces to messengers and sent them all over Israel with this warning: "Anyone who does not come and follow Saul and Samuel into battle will have his oxen cut up like these." {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} made the people afraid, so they all came out together, united as one.

decisions.choice: cut them in pieces and sent them through all the territory of Israel: a summons like the one in Judges 19
decisions.reason: The Levite of Judges 19:29 cut up his concubine's body and sent the pieces through all the territory of Israel, and Israel gathered against Gibeah in Benjamin. Now a man of Gibeah sends pieces of his oxen to call Israel together, this time to rescue a town rather than to punish one.

decisions.choice: whoever does not come out ... so will it be done to his cattle: a threat that backs the call to arms
decisions.reason: The cut pieces show what will happen to the livestock of anyone who ignores the summons. For a farmer, losing his oxen meant losing his living. "Come out after" means to go out to war following a leader.

decisions.choice: the dread of the LORD: a fear sent by Yahweh
alternatives: fear of what the LORD would do to them
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean a terror that Yahweh brings on people (Genesis 35:5 uses a similar phrase for a terror from God on the towns around Jacob). Here it moves Israel to obey the summons at once, a sign that Yahweh is behind Saul.

decisions.choice: as one man: all together, in full agreement
decisions.reason: The phrase describes the whole people acting as a single body, as when Israel gathered in Judges 20:1, 8, 11.

decisions.choice: into battle
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that "come out after" a leader means going out to fight.

decisions.choice: the LORD made the people afraid
decisions.reason: Readable turns "the dread of the LORD fell on the people" into a plain statement that the fear came from Yahweh, following the reading in the meaning decision above.

records.source: וַֽיִּפְקְדֵ֖ם בְּבָ֑זֶק וַיִּהְי֤וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ שְׁלֹ֣שׁ מֵא֣וֹת אֶ֔לֶף וְאִ֥ישׁ יְהוּדָ֖ה שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים אָֽלֶף׃
records.gloss: And he mustered them at Bezek, and were [the] sons of Israel three hundred thousand, and [the] men of Judah thirty thousand.
pieces: When Saul counted them at Bezek, the men of Israel numbered 300,000, and the men of Judah 30,000.

L.8: And he mustered them at Bezek, and the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel were 300,000, and the men of Judah 30,000.

R.8: Saul gathered and counted the army at Bezek. There were 300,000 men from Israel and 30,000 from Judah.

decisions.choice: Bezek: a place west of the Jordan facing Jabesh-gilead
decisions.reason: Bezek lay in the hills west of the Jordan, across the valley from Jabesh-gilead. From there an army could cross and reach the town in a night's march (verse 11).

decisions.choice: thousand: the figures may be counts of units rather than of men
decisions.reason: As in the census lists of Numbers (see the note at Numbers 1:21), the word for "thousand" can also name a military or clan unit, which would make the army much smaller than the figures suggest.

decisions.choice: three hundred thousand and thirty thousand
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text gives these figures. The old Greek translation has larger ones (600,000 for Israel and 70,000 for Judah), and a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel also has 70,000 for Judah. Reviewers should check the witnesses.

decisions.choice: Israel ... Judah: the tribes counted in two groups
decisions.reason: Judah is listed apart from the rest of Israel, as it is again in 15:4 and 17:52. The split looks ahead to the two kingdoms that later formed (1 Kings 12).

decisions.choice: the men of Israel (Balanced); men from Israel (Readable)
decisions.reason: The phrase is literally "the sons of Israel". In an army count it means the fighting men, so Balanced and Readable say "men" with no gender setting; Literal keeps the usual setting for the phrase.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ לַמַּלְאָכִ֣ים הַבָּאִ֗ים כֹּ֤ה תֹֽאמְרוּן֙ לְאִישׁ֙ יָבֵ֣ישׁ גִּלְעָ֔ד מָחָ֛ר תִּהְיֶֽה־לָכֶ֥ם תְּשׁוּעָ֖ה כְּחֹ֣ם הַשָּׁ֑מֶשׁ וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ הַמַּלְאָכִ֗ים וַיַּגִּ֛ידוּ לְאַנְשֵׁ֥י יָבֵ֖ישׁ וַיִּשְׂמָֽחוּ׃
records.gloss: And they said to the messengers who had come, Thus you will say to [the] men of Jabesh-gilead, Tomorrow there will be to you deliverance, when [the] sun [is] hot. And came the messengers and told [the] men of Jabesh, and they rejoiced.
pieces: They told the messengers who had come, "Say to the men of Jabesh-gilead, 'Rescue will come to you tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot.'" When the messengers went back and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad.

L.9: And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus you will say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, when the sun is hot, there will be deliverance for you.'" And the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, and they rejoiced.

R.9: They told the messengers from Jabesh, "Go back and tell the men of Jabesh-gilead, 'Tomorrow, before the day gets hot, you will be rescued.'" The messengers went and gave them the news, and the men of Jabesh were full of joy.

decisions.choice: they said: Saul and the leaders with him
decisions.reason: The verb is plural and no subject is named. The ones who speak are those who have just gathered the army, Saul with Samuel (verse 7) and the leaders of the people.

decisions.choice: deliverance: rescue from the enemy
decisions.reason: The word is related to the verb "save" in verse 3. The elders had asked whether anyone would save them; now the answer comes. Saul uses the same word in verse 13, where he says it is Yahweh who brought it.

decisions.choice: when the sun is hot: by late morning or midday
decisions.reason: The heat of the sun marks the time of day, as "the heat of the day" does in verse 11 and Genesis 18:1. The attack will be over before noon.

decisions.choice: from Jabesh ... Go back
decisions.reason: Readable says where the messengers came from and that they returned there, which the story implies.

records.source: וַֽיֹּאמְרוּ֙ אַנְשֵׁ֣י יָבֵ֔ישׁ מָחָ֖ר נֵצֵ֣א אֲלֵיכֶ֑ם וַעֲשִׂיתֶ֣ם לָּ֔נוּ כְּכָל־הַטּ֖וֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶֽם׃ס
records.gloss: And said [the] men of Jabesh, Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you will do to us according to all the good in your eyes.
pieces: Then the men of Jabesh said to the Ammonites, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do with us whatever you think best."

L.10: And the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us according to all that is good in your eyes."

R.10: Then the men of Jabesh sent word to the Ammonites, "Tomorrow we will come out to you. Then you can do whatever you want with us."

decisions.choice: you: Nahash and his army
decisions.reason: The "you" is plural. The men of Jabesh are speaking to the Ammonites, though the verse does not name them.

decisions.choice: we will come out to you: words with a double meaning
decisions.reason: The Ammonites would hear an offer to surrender, as in verse 3. The men of Jabesh know they will come out to fight once Saul's army arrives. The pretense keeps the Ammonites off guard.

decisions.choice: all that is good in your eyes: whatever you think best
decisions.reason: "Good in your eyes" means what seems right to someone. Here it means "whatever you like".

decisions.choice: to the Ammonites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name whom the men of Jabesh were speaking to; Readable also says they "sent word", since the town was still under siege.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י מִֽמָּחֳרָ֗ת וַיָּ֨שֶׂם שָׁא֣וּל אֶת־הָעָם֮ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה רָאשִׁים֒ וַיָּבֹ֤אוּ בְתוֹךְ־הַֽמַּחֲנֶה֙ בְּאַשְׁמֹ֣רֶת הַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיַּכּ֥וּ אֶת־עַמּ֖וֹן עַד־חֹ֣ם הַיּ֑וֹם וַיְהִ֤י הַנִּשְׁאָרִים֙ וַיָּפֻ֔צוּ וְלֹ֥א נִשְׁאֲרוּ־בָ֖ם שְׁנַ֥יִם יָֽחַד׃
records.gloss: And it was on [the] next day, and set Saul the people [in] three companies, and they came into [the] midst of the camp in [the] watch of the morning and struck Ammon until [the] heat of the day; and it was, those remaining were scattered, and not remained among them two together.
pieces: The next day Saul arranged the army in three companies. During the morning watch they broke into the camp and cut down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. The survivors were scattered so widely that no two of them were left together.

L.11: And it was on the next day, and Saul set the people in three companies, and they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch, and struck down Ammon until the heat of the day. And it was, those who remained were scattered, and there did not remain among them two together.

R.11: The next day Saul split his army into three groups. In the last hours before dawn they broke into the Ammonite camp, and they kept killing Ammonites until the middle of the day. The ones who lived ran off in every direction, and no two of them were left together.

decisions.choice: three companies: a tactic for attacking from several sides
decisions.reason: Gideon divided his men into three companies for his night attack on Midian (Judges 7:16), and Abimelech did the same (Judges 9:43). The word for "companies" is literally "heads". "The people" here means the army, as often in Samuel.

decisions.choice: the morning watch: the last part of the night, before sunrise
decisions.reason: The night was divided into watches. The morning watch was the last, before dawn, when an army in camp would least expect an attack (Exodus 14:24).

decisions.choice: not two together: the enemy was completely broken up
decisions.reason: The survivors fled in such disorder that no two of them stayed together. The Ammonite army no longer existed as a fighting force.

decisions.choice: the army; the Ammonites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "army" for "the people" because the context is a battle, and "the Ammonites" for "Ammon", the nation named for the people.

decisions.choice: in the last hours before dawn; until the middle of the day
decisions.reason: Readable explains the watch and the heat of the day as times a modern reader can picture.

records.heading: Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָעָם֙ אֶל־שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל מִ֣י הָאֹמֵ֔ר שָׁא֖וּל יִמְלֹ֣ךְ עָלֵ֑ינוּ תְּנ֥וּ הָאֲנָשִׁ֖ים וּנְמִיתֵֽם׃
records.gloss: And said the people to Samuel, Who [is] the [one] saying, Saul will reign over us? Give the men, and we will put them to death.
pieces: Then the people said to Samuel, "Who were the ones who said, 'Is Saul to reign over us?' Hand those men over, and we will put them to death."

L.12: And the people said to Samuel, "Who [is] the one who said, 'Saul will reign over us?' Give [us] the men, and we will put them to death."

R.12: Then the people said to Samuel, "Who asked, 'Is Saul really going to be our king?' Hand those men over to us, and we will kill them."

decisions.choice: the ones who said, 'Is Saul to reign over us?': the men who despised Saul at his choosing
decisions.reason: At Mizpah some worthless men had scorned Saul, saying, "How can this man save us?" and brought him no gift (10:27). Now that Saul has saved Jabesh, the people want those men punished.

decisions.choice: Saul will reign over us?: a scornful question with no question word
alternatives: a statement: Saul will reign over us
decisions.reason: Hebrew can ask a question by tone of voice alone. The words repeat the doubters' mocking question, as if to say "Is Saul going to be king over us?" It could also be read as a statement quoted back in scorn; either way the people mean the men who refused Saul.

decisions.choice: the men: those particular men
decisions.reason: The article points back to the men of 10:27, not to men in general.

decisions.choice: hand over
decisions.reason: The verb is literally "give". In a demand for people to be punished it means to hand them over, as in Judges 20:13.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֔וּל לֹֽא־יוּמַ֥ת אִ֖ישׁ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּ֥י הַיּ֛וֹם עָשָֽׂה־יְהוָ֥ה תְּשׁוּעָ֖ה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ס
records.gloss: And said Saul, Not will be put to death a man on this day, for today has worked Yahweh deliverance in Israel.
pieces: But Saul said, "No one will be put to death today, for today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has brought deliverance to Israel."

L.13: And Saul said, "No man will be put to death on this day, for today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has worked deliverance in Israel."

R.13: But Saul said, "No one will be put to death today, because today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has rescued Israel."

decisions.choice: the LORD has worked deliverance: the victory is credited to Yahweh
decisions.reason: Saul does not claim the rescue for himself. He names Yahweh as the one who saved Israel, as Jonathan does at Michmash (14:6, 45) and as Samuel insists in 12:7-11.

decisions.choice: no one will be put to death today: a day of victory is not spoiled by revenge
decisions.reason: A day on which Yahweh has saved his people is kept for joy, not for executions of fellow Israelites. David shows the same restraint toward Shimei on the day of his return (2 Samuel 19:23).

decisions.choice: deliverance: as in verse 9
decisions.reason: The promise of verse 9 has come true, and Saul says whose doing it was.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵל֙ אֶל־הָעָ֔ם לְכ֖וּ וְנֵלְכָ֣ה הַגִּלְגָּ֑ל וּנְחַדֵּ֥שׁ שָׁ֖ם הַמְּלוּכָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Samuel to the people, Come, and let us go [to] Gilgal and let us renew there the kingship.
pieces: Samuel then told the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingship."

L.14: And Samuel said to the people, "Come, and let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there."

R.14: Samuel told the people, "Come with me to Gilgal. There we will confirm once more that Saul is our king."

decisions.choice: renew the kingship: confirm Saul's rule now that the whole people accepts it
alternatives: make the kingship new: begin Saul's reign in practice
decisions.reason: Saul had been chosen by lot and acclaimed at Mizpah (10:17-25), but some had rejected him (10:27). After the victory the people gather again to confirm the kingship publicly, with every doubt removed. The word "renew" may also mean to restore or to start afresh; either way it is the same kingship, not a new one.

decisions.choice: Gilgal: an old sanctuary near the Jordan
decisions.reason: Gilgal was where Israel first camped in the land and set up the twelve stones (Joshua 4:19-20; 5:9-10). It was one of the places Samuel judged Israel each year (7:16), and Samuel had told Saul to wait for him there (10:8).

decisions.choice: confirm once more that Saul is our king
decisions.reason: Readable explains "renew the kingship" by naming Saul and what the gathering did. It follows the main reading in the meaning decision above.

records.heading: The kingship renewed at Gilgal

records.source: וַיֵּלְכ֨וּ כָל־הָעָ֜ם הַגִּלְגָּ֗ל וַיַּמְלִכוּ֩ שָׁ֨ם אֶת־שָׁא֜וּל לִפְנֵ֤י יְהוָה֙ בַּגִּלְגָּ֔ל וַיִּזְבְּחוּ־שָׁ֛ם זְבָחִ֥ים שְׁלָמִ֖ים לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיִּשְׂמַ֨ח שָׁ֥ם שָׁא֛וּל וְכָל־אַנְשֵׁ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עַד־מְאֹֽד׃פ
records.gloss: And went all the people [to] Gilgal, and made king there Saul before Yahweh in Gilgal, and sacrificed there sacrifices of peace offerings before Yahweh; and rejoiced there Saul and all [the] men of Israel exceedingly.
pieces: So all the people went to Gilgal, and there, in the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Gilgal, they made Saul king. They offered peace offerings there before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and Saul and all the men of Israel celebrated with great joy.

L.15: And all the people went to Gilgal, and they made Saul king there before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} in Gilgal, and they sacrificed there sacrifices of peace offerings before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. And Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced there greatly.

R.15: So all the people went to Gilgal. There, in the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, they made Saul their king. They offered peace offerings to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and Saul and all the men of Israel were filled with joy.

decisions.choice: they made Saul king before the LORD: the people confirm Saul as king in Yahweh's presence
decisions.reason: "Before the LORD" means at the sanctuary, as an act done in Yahweh's sight. The people make Saul king, but they do it before the God who chose him (10:24).

decisions.choice: sacrifices of peace offerings: offerings shared in a meal
decisions.reason: In a peace offering part of the animal was burned on the altar and the rest was eaten by the worshipers, a feast of fellowship before God (Leviticus 3; 7:11-15). It suits a day of celebration.

decisions.choice: Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly: the chapter ends in shared joy
decisions.reason: The joy of Jabesh in verse 9 spreads to the whole people. The next chapter turns to Samuel's warning about what the kingship will require (12:1-25).

decisions.choice: offered peace offerings
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "sacrificed sacrifices of peace offerings". Balanced and Readable give the sense once, with the usual name "peace offerings" kept at every level.
